summary: Adds IPv6 support to TURN, including relaying between IPv4 and IPv6, and defines the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute for choosing the address type. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 8656.

eli5.summary: A relay helps two devices behind walls reach each other. This teaches the helper to work with both old and new address types.

can turn relay between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: IPv6 support for TURN relay servers, including cross-version relaying.

tldr.problem: TURN allows devices behind restrictive NATs to receive traffic through a relay server, but only supported IPv4. Applications needed to relay between IPv4 and IPv6 or allocate IPv6 addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6156 adds IPv6 support to TURN through the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute, which lets clients ask for IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. The relay translates packet headers when crossing between IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now mix IPv4 and IPv6 using TURN relays, and servers can translate between versions. This was later updated by RFC 8656, which consolidated TURN specifications.

today: RFC 6156 added IPv6 support to TURN in 2011. It was later superseded by RFC 8656, which consolidated TURN specifications and includes the IPv6 extensions. The mechanisms defined here—particularly the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute and cross-version translation rules—remain part of the modern TURN specification.

sections.title: TURN and the Need for IPv6
sections.content:
TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) is defined in RFC 5766. It helps devices that are stuck behind Network Address Translators (NATs) to receive incoming traffic. A device asks a TURN server to allocate a relay address, and other devices send data to that relay address instead. The relay forwards the traffic back to the requesting device.

The original TURN specification only handled IPv4-to-IPv4 relaying. As IPv6 became more common, applications needed TURN to work with IPv6 addresses, and to bridge between clients on different versions of the protocol.

RFC 6156 adds full IPv6 support to TURN, including the ability to allocate IPv6 addresses, relay between IPv4 and IPv6, and relay between two IPv6 hosts.
sections.eli5: A relay in an old system only knew how to pass messages between IPv4 addresses. This extension teaches it to understand IPv6 addresses too, and to translate between the two.

sections.title: Requesting an Address Type
sections.content:
To allocate a relayed address, a client sends an Allocate request to the TURN server. RFC 6156 adds a new REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute to this request.

The attribute specifies whether the client wants an IPv4 address (0x01) or an IPv6 address (0x02). If the client does not include this attribute, the server allocates an IPv4 address by default. The server returns the allocated address in an XOR-RELAYED-ADDRESS attribute in the response.

If the server does not support the requested address family, it responds with error code 440 (Address Family not Supported). This tells the client not to retry; the server simply cannot provide that address type.
sections.eli5: The client tells the server: 'I want an IPv4 address' or 'I want an IPv6 address.' The server picks a free address of that type and hands it back.

sections.title: Cross-Version Relay Operation
sections.content:
Once an allocation is set up, the client can use TURN to relay traffic. The TURN server translates packets between the client and peer addresses.

When relaying between different versions, the server must translate not just IP addresses but also header fields. For IPv4-to-IPv6 translation, the relay must set the IPv6 Traffic Class, Flow Label, and Hop Limit fields according to rules from RFC 6145. For IPv6-to-IPv4 translation, it must set the Type of Service and Time to Live fields similarly.

For IPv6-to-IPv6 relaying, the relay does not copy the Flow Label from the incoming packet, because it represents two separate flows. The relay also handles fragmentation, generating ICMP Packet Too Big messages when packets exceed the link MTU.

The specification provides preferred and alternate behaviors: servers SHOULD implement the preferred approach (which follows RFC 6145 for translation rules) but MAY use simpler alternate approaches if needed.
sections.eli5: When the relay passes a message from one version to another, it has to rewrite some parts of the address envelope—like the time-to-live counter—because they work differently.

sections.title: Permissions and Channels
sections.content:
TURN uses two mechanisms to send traffic: Send indications (for one-off messages) and Channels (for ongoing communication).

When a client creates a permission or channel, it specifies the peer address. RFC 6156 adds a new rule: the peer address family MUST match the family of the relayed address. If they do not match, the server returns error code 443 (Peer Address Family Mismatch).

For example, if a client allocated an IPv6 relayed address but tries to create a permission for an IPv4 peer, the server rejects the request. This ensures the relay can always translate between the relayed address and the peer address.
sections.eli5: If your relay address is IPv6, your peer must be IPv6. If it is IPv4, your peer must be IPv4. You cannot mix them in a single permission or channel.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
IPv4-to-IPv6 relaying creates new security concerns. An IPv4-only client can now access IPv6 networks through the TURN server, and vice versa. This must be considered when setting security policies and monitoring rules for the server.

The loop attack described in RFC 5766 (where an attacker tricks the relay into forwarding traffic back to itself) can be easier to perform over IPv6 if address spoofing is simpler in the network. However, the mitigation is the same: careful validation of traffic flows.

All security considerations from RFC 5389 (STUN) and RFC 5766 (TURN) continue to apply. The translation itself does not introduce new cryptographic weaknesses.
sections.eli5: Now that the relay can connect IPv4 and IPv6 networks, the server administrator needs to think about whether that connection should be allowed. The basic safety of the relay protocol itself doesn't change.
